hints: Apply Newton's second law to the whole system of mass $3600 + 1200 = 4800\text{ kg}$ to find acceleration: $2500 - (700 + 300) = 4800a$.
Once acceleration $a$ is found, apply Newton's second law to the trailer ($1200\text{ kg}$) alone: $T - 300 = 1200a$, and solve for tension T.
walkthrough:
Apply Newton's second law to the entire van and trailer system:
$$F_D - R_{\text{total}} = (m_{\text{van}} + m_{\text{trailer}})a$$
$$2500 - (700 + 300) = (3600 + 1200)a$$
$$1500 = 4800a \implies a = \frac{1500}{4800} = \frac{5}{16} = 0.3125\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Apply Newton's second law to the trailer ($m = 1200\text{ kg}$, resistance $300\text{ N}$):
$$T - 300 = 1200a = 1200(0.3125) = 375$$
$$T = 300 + 375 = 675\text{ N}$$

ai_rubric.Solving Connected-Particle Systems: Finds system acceleration $a = 0.3125\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and trailer tension $T = 675\text{ N}$.

teacher_walkthrough:
State Newton's second law for the connected van and trailer system moving along the horizontal road:
$$\sum F = m_{\text{total}} a$$
Identify the parameters:
- Mass of van: $m_{\text{van}} = 3600\text{ kg}$
- Mass of trailer: $m_{\text{trailer}} = 1200\text{ kg}$
- Total mass: $m_{\text{total}} = 3600 + 1200 = 4800\text{ kg}$
- Forward driving force on van: $F_D = 2500\text{ N}$
- Total backward resistance: $R_{\text{total}} = 700 + 300 = 1000\text{ N}$

Set up the equation of motion for the system:
$$F_D - R_{\text{total}} = m_{\text{total}} a$$
$$2500 - 1000 = 4800a$$
$$1500 = 4800a$$
Divide both sides by $4800$:
$$a = \frac{1500}{4800} = \frac{5}{16} = 0.3125\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Isolate the trailer to determine the tension $T$ in the tow-rope. The forces acting horizontally on the trailer are:
- Forward pulling tension: $T$
- Backward resistance: $300\text{ N}$
Apply Newton's second law to the trailer:
$$T - 300 = m_{\text{trailer}} a$$
Substitute $m_{\text{trailer}} = 1200\text{ kg}$ and $a = 0.3125\text{ m s}^{-2}$:
$$T - 300 = 1200(0.3125) = 375$$
Add $300$ to both sides:
$$T = 300 + 375 = 675\text{ N}$$
Thus the tension in the rope is $675\text{ N}$.

hints: When the rope becomes slack, the tension drops to zero ($T = 0$).
Under its own resistance of $300\text{ N}$ alone, the trailer has acceleration $a = -\frac{300}{1200} = -0.25\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
For the rope to become slack, the van must decelerate at least as fast as the trailer ($a_{\text{van}} \le -0.25$). Set up $-F - 700 = 3600(-0.25)$ and solve for the least braking force F.
walkthrough:
Find the deceleration of the trailer when the rope becomes slack ($T = 0$):
$$-300 = 1200 a_{\text{trailer}} \implies a_{\text{trailer}} = -\frac{300}{1200} = -0.25\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

For the rope to become slack, the van must decelerate at least as rapidly as the trailer ($a_{\text{van}} \le -0.25\text{ m s}^{-2}$):
$$-F - 700 = 3600(-0.25)$$
$$-F - 700 = -900$$
$$F = 900 - 700 = 200\text{ N}$$

ai_rubric.Solving Connected-Particle Systems: Sets $T = 0$, finds trailer acceleration $-0.25\text{ m s}^{-2}$, and solves $-F - 700 = 3600(-0.25)$ to obtain $F = 200\text{ N}$.

teacher_walkthrough: Understand the condition for the rope to become slack: a light flexible rope cannot sustain compression. It becomes slack whenever the tension reduces to zero ($T = 0$) and the leading vehicle decelerates at least as quickly as the trailing vehicle.

Consider the trailer when the rope is slack ($T = 0$): the only horizontal force acting on the trailer is its natural resistance $R_{\text{trailer}} = 300\text{ N}$ opposing motion:
$$-300 = m_{\text{trailer}} a$$
$$-300 = 1200a \implies a = -\frac{300}{1200} = -0.25\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

For the rope to become slack, the van acceleration $a_{\text{van}}$ must satisfy $a_{\text{van}} \le -0.25\text{ m s}^{-2}$. The forces acting on the van with braking force $F$ and natural resistance $700\text{ N}$ are:
$$-F - 700 = m_{\text{van}} a_{\text{van}}$$
For the least braking force, set $a_{\text{van}} = -0.25\text{ m s}^{-2}$:
$$-F - 700 = 3600(-0.25)$$
$$-F - 700 = -900$$
Multiply through by $-1$:
$$F + 700 = 900$$
Subtract $700$ from both sides:
$$F = 900 - 700 = 200\text{ N}$$
Thus the least possible value of the braking force is $200\text{ N}$.
